html:
The Second Battle of the Marne was fought from 15 July to early August 1918 around the Marne River and Reims, in northeast France. It was the last German offensive of World War I, and the Allied counter-attack that followed turned the war.

Russia had left the war, and Germany moved its armies west to win before American troops arrived in strength. Four attacks from March 1918 gained ground but not victory. On 15 July Erich Ludendorff struck on both sides of Reims. East of the city the French knew the plan and stopped the attack in a day. To the west the Germans crossed the Marne but could go no further. On 18 July the Allied commander Ferdinand Foch hit their flank near Soissons with French and American divisions and about 350 tanks, without warning. The Germans fell back behind the Aisne and Vesle rivers.

Germany lost about 168,000 men and the Allies about 133,000, most of them from France. Ludendorff cancelled his next offensive and never attacked again. The United States now had over a million soldiers in France. The Battle of Amiens came next, four years after the first battle on the same river.
